@keon.kineki  You’re trying really hard to sound smart, but most of what you wrote falls apart the moment you actually think about it.

“You should be able to defend your stance no matter the questions” only works in a fair debate. If the questions are biased, one-sided, or poorly constructed, that doesn’t test truth, it tests patience. A bad moderator can make even a strong position look weak. That’s not a gotcha, that’s just basic logic.

You also act like struggling in a chaotic discussion automatically means the argument is weak. No. It often means the discussion itself is garbage. When people interrupt each other, talk over one another, and there’s no structure or control, that’s not a debate, that’s noise. And noise doesn’t prove anyone right.

Then there’s your “freedom” argument. You throw that word around like it automatically gives you the moral high ground. It doesn’t. Not every movement that claims “freedom” is automatically right or beyond criticism. History is full of people fighting for things that made no sense or led to worse outcomes.

You accuse me of generalizing, while doing the exact same thing. Yes, there are women who succeed in physically demanding jobs, just like there are men who fail them. That’s obvious. But exceptions don’t disprove general trends. On average, men have higher physical strength. That’s not sexism, that’s biology. Ignoring that doesn’t make you enlightened, it just makes you dishonest.

Your point about education is ironic. Understanding social movements is part of being educated, sure. But so is critical thinking. Blindly agreeing with something because it sounds morally nice isn’t intelligence, it’s conformity.

And the whole “Czech Republic vs US” thing — you completely missed the point. No one said problems elsewhere should be ignored. The point is that not every society is dealing with the same issues in the same way. Acting like one country’s problems automatically apply everywhere is narrow thinking.

Lastly, calling me angry or bitter isn’t an argument. It’s just a way to avoid actually responding to what was said. Labeling someone doesn’t make you right, it just shows you ran out of real points.

You’re trying to turn this into an emotional story about oppression and morality, but reality is simpler: a weak debate doesn’t prove a strong ideology, loud people don’t equal correct people, and feelings don’t replace facts.

Memorization is a skill. Debate itself requires skill (many skills, in fact), but your debate skill is not a measure of the FACTS. Debates like these are well-known for being full of rhetorical traps and tricks. If anything, that means that having notes helps to keep you ON POINT, ON TOPIC, and ON THE FACTS. You should be encouraging notes -- facts that can be referenced and dissected -- over public speaking skills.

Our drywall team is extremely diverse (women, men, Spanish, Russian, etc), and some of our more "old-school" employees have a harder time with the adjustment, but it really does seem to come down to just having a conversation about it. I know one of our younger female employees experienced more than once was "tickling" on the job site. Our rule is "Just don't touch each other unless you are getting tools from each other, or shaking someone's hand". There definitely is a big adjustment to having men and women on the job site. We have had to make the "line" between friendliness and joking, and actually flirting very clear (as in she's probably not flirting). Honestly, though, we hardly see this being an issue anymore on the jobsites we are on, which is really great!

We need to find a less toxic approach to what is admittedly a necessary conversation or I fear fewer, not more, women will find there way into board rooms. I suppose Sam, whom I have greatly admired, will want to castrate me for expressing this view. I can’t help but feel or sense that Sam sees little redeeming value in the male gender. text:
I think there's a disconnect in how people are approaching this. When someone says "toxic masculinity doesn't exist, only toxic individuals," they're missing the point that we're talking about cultural patterns of behavior, not claiming all masculinity is toxic.

Toxic masculinity refers to specific learned behaviors that get associated with "being a man" - like the idea that asking for help is weak, that you should never show emotion except anger, or that dominance is how you prove yourself. These aren't innate to being male; they're cultural messages that harm both the men who feel pressured to perform them and the people around them.

Saying "only the individual is toxic" ignores how these patterns get reinforced and passed down. Individual people do choose their behaviors, but those choices don't happen in a vacuum - they're influenced by what they've been taught "real men" do.

The term isn't saying masculinity itself is bad. It's identifying which specific expectations and behaviors cause harm so we can separate those from healthier ways of being masculine. You can absolutely be masculine without the toxic parts.

As for the "if toxic masculinity exists, then so does toxic femininity" argument - yes, actually, toxic femininity is also a real thing. It includes harmful patterns like the expectation that women must be endlessly nurturing at their own expense, that they should be passive or manipulative rather than direct, or that their worth is primarily tied to appearance and pleasing others. Both concepts exist because both genders face harmful cultural expectations. Acknowledging one doesn't deny the other.

But voting is NOT the only important element here.  If you fail to register, you can have your immigration status revoked.  You can lose out on Pell grants (hey buddy, this is that college thing I was talking about!  Actual systemic barriers for those who need the help!  You do know what a Pell grant is right?), and even if you're a conscientious objector, you still have to register before you can declare that in the event of an actual draft.  People are quick to be all like, "the last one was in the 70's hurrrrrr", but a lot of people alive today lost their best friends on the battlefield in Vietnam.  I know men whose lives have been ruined by Agent Orange.  A lot of Vietnamese people are alive today that lost entire segments of their family during that campaign.  Are those lives so meaningless to you that you'd wash your hands of the whole thing and act like the possibility of that happening again is ignorable?  Let alone what veterans face in this country, and faced then.  You are hopelessly out of touch to suggest that young men don't fear a war with Iran because what it comes down to, is the boomer generation playing war with our lives.  That's not my fault bucko.  Doesn't matter how many men make that call, I am not a responsible figure there.  How do you reconcile that cognitive dissonance?  Where you blame men for what other men do?  You know, that part where you wave aside any criticism by saying the evil menz did it, with no acknowledgment or acceptance for the roles women do in fact play in these fields, and always have.  It takes a rather narrow lens on history to simplify it that poorly.  Here's a pro-tip friend; America is not the entire world.  Read up a bit on what the rest of the world was doing before and during the American Empire.  You'll find plenty of female warriors in history.

Oh but hey, we still haven't covered all the problems with SSS!  If you fail to register, you're eligible to receive five years of prison!  And 250,000 in fines!  Come on down, contestant!  You can Since you seem to be that much of a clueless fuck about what men and women actually do with their lives and why they cave into these pressures.  Maybe if we apply the word sexism to everything we'll shit out an answer that way, but I would think looking at employment data and family statistics is a pretty decent way to picture what men and women's priorities are, and why they make the choices men and women have to reach out in different directions.  In my place of employment, that means taking a tiny woman seriously in a heavy labor job.  Turns out she's actually something of a machine, but had I and others not encouraged her, she would never have lasted long enough to find out.  I believe that social pressures make a difference here, but feminists are too quick to chant the culture mantra to realize that there are actual practical ways to change the landscape of gender roles in America and at large.  Instead we get Ban Bossy and Beyonce using the feminist label for record sales (to almost nobody's chagrin).  We get Take Back The Night, despite the overwhelming majority of rape being via acquaintance (which such a campaign does not enlighten potential victims about, which disservices them).  I'd like to take this moment to assure you that I don't blame female students for the decline in male college attendance, I blame factors at every step of education and the systemic barriers that are out of the reach of students.

I'm saying these things because feminism is off-base, off point, and doesn't actually accomplish much of anything these days.  And those feminists that do, do so almost exclusively for the benefit of women.  Invariably, this leaves men and male victims out in the cold, sometimes disproportionately worse than their female counterparts.  As someone who cares about suicide, mental illness, homelessness, and a myriad of other concerns, I don't see these as gendered phenomena, not exclusively at least.  They're human concerns, but feminist rhetoric does not take into account male humanity.  We are rapists, oppressors, hateful bigots and chauvinists.  They point to the apex males of society and claim the rest of us have everything.  Never mind that these accusations apply to a tiny fraction of the population and the majority of men out there are entirely divorced from the corporate CEO's and moves-makers.  You are willing to look past that something is wrong, and needs to be changed, because apparently some men created the rule, therefore all men are responsible.  You're a fucking sexist, just own up to it already.  Your double standards are obvious.

of paying attention.  This leads many teachers to unfairly grade their male students on behavior as opposed to comprehension, putting large swaths of men into academic categories that harm them.  For example, young boys who struggle to sit still in math class end up prescribed ADHD medicines and get placed in lower math classes, to be sometimes years behind their female peers.  I knew handfuls of close personal friends in high school who had this exact problem.  They did not actually have ADHD, but sexist teachers pressured their parents into that interpretation.  And do you think psychiatrists are trying to let go of that kind of cash cow?  Parents who aren't willing to even be parents are willing to toss cash away to "solve the problem".  Because normal male behavior is seen as problematic in our society.  Great message to send to young boys at a time when their minds might still be fertile.  Then in high school they get constant shaming for their sexuality (from all angles, women are just as bad if not worse about this than men are), and the continuous belief that their normal behaviors are toxic.  By the time a boy has been through 12 years of this shit, the likelihood of him going to college (and succeeding) instead of taking the 10-15 an hour labor job is minimal.  He can lift things, but nobody believed in him enough to teach him differential equations.  That's your prototypical American male youth.  Deck stacked against him from the outright, persecuted for his "privilege" (which is a murky, amorphous, undefined term in most conversations, useless for examination) and we aren't even talking about actual personal issues that might interfere too.  For me, the breadwinner of the house died.  I got a stark reminder that if I can't provide (or make enough money to afford a good life insurance policy), then I will leave my future family all alone to fend for themselves, a gigantic source of personal doubt and guilt.  Men are not encouraged to be open about these problems.  I will get accusations of crying on this post.  I haven't even died and that shit makes me feel guilty.  Imagine the pressures young men face at home, in their community, in the classroom, amongst their peers.  How many young children deal with single parents because of our corrupt Prison Industrial Complex?  We talk endlessly about the female perspective there, but act like young men aren't feeling human beings like everyone else.  Why is that?  Why do feminists feel so threatened when you emphasize male humanity?  Are they scared that men will want to be equal too?  Because what feminists claim men have is supremacy, despite that belonging to a fraction of a percent of humanity, let alone men.  Do feminists want superiority?  They already have all of the freedoms men have, and all of the legal rights, and more.  Feminists either want genuine equality (not equity, equality) or they want supremacy.  There is no middle ground.

Feminists can't take up every suicide statistic?  I'm sure they can't.  But they made some pretty big promises to trans people out there.  Feminists offered to open their umbrella, and take them in.  Feminist circles called these people their brothers and sisters, and left them out in the cold.  You cannot justify how they fell through.  You probably don't even know about it, which I can't fault you on, most trans issues do not see the light of discussion.  Having been suicidal myself before, I took a special interest in the statistic.  Because anything (in their case, usually dysphoria) that can create a near half rate of suicide is absolutely appalling and demands more serious attention.  Where's the need you say?  Right fucking there.  That's a serious issue that demands immediate attention.  But instead, feminists wait for a trans person to kill themselves.  Then they swoop in for the publicity, crying out against the pressures that caused it but not accurately identifying them.  They will use examples where the deceased have written letters that detail bullying, when hundreds of others did so because there are serious barriers to transitioning, the medically necessary procedure that saves trans people's lives.  And then there's the identity politics crowd (mostly Tumblrites) who adopt countless labels and for some reason believe this makes them trans, appropriating the label, shoving trans concerns even further under the rug.  Believe me, you have to see this stuff for yourself before you can get to the point where you've lost faith in these feminists.  You can't just look past feminists who tell these individuals to kill themselves, because heaven forbid a trans person's perspective might be slightly different than feminist rhetoric.  Particularly trans exclusive radical feminists (affectionately called TERFs), who wont even recognize the gender that trans people know themselves to be.  But where are the feminists decrying these actions?  Nofuckingwhere to be found.  Ever.  I will see posts that get 300,000 notifications, and only find five feminists who had anything to say against it.  That's bad.  That's outright awful, and there's so much infighting in the movement that nobody even agrees upon what it is in the first place.  How is that kind of movement effective?  How can they help women, let alone help all of us reach equality?  How can that kind of group even agree upon what equality means?

You asked if MRA's have helped trans people.  Well, they aren't really organized enough to put up huge gains, but in some small ways yes they have.  To start with, advocating on behalf of shorter wait times for procedures.  Because trans trending is literally a thing (some feminists believe that oppression=social power, because you can claim authority if you can claim to face the most oppressions, aka oppression olympics), doctors have extended wait times from 6 months to a year for procedures to go underway.  This is a huge issue because of that suicide rate, which might get worse if people have to hold out longer.  MRA's have offered general support for individuals scorned by feminists, and have defended them in many different places.  Where feminists have excluded trans men (for being, I shit you not, "gender traitors"), MRA's have welcomed them with open arms, more concerned with their experiences as males than as their dysphoric experiences while presenting female.  Regardless, MRA's care more about you being male (and what that implies for you socially, culturally, systemically) than about traditionalism or traditional roles.  Where feminists get the impression that MRA's are traditionalists is beyond me.  Maybe because they associate opponents to their rhetoric as being conservative?  I'm a liberal, so I'm on the receiving end of a lot of these accusations.  Feminists just flat out don't like most MRA's, period.  And if feminists stopped protesting MRA events, maybe that movement could get off the ground and then we could stop arguing about how feminists have left men in the dust.  After all, MRA's have no lobbying power, no funding, no significant cultural influence, etc.  So give them time to make better advocacy, they're working on limited resources.

But I'm not really an MRA.  I'm an egalitarian.  I'm a humanist.  I am an antifeminist.  And you sir, are clueless about the bill of goods you've been sold.  Fine man, be a sock puppet.  I'd rather think for myself, attempt to persuade with facts not allegory, and push information as weaponry over bigotry.  Go your own way and keep insisting feminists are both responsible and not responsible for everything (funny how you change tunes based on convenience).  How does that work anyway?  Feminists did everything for women, but aren't responsible for playing a role in making things better for men too?  They needed men to make that happen, and men let it happen.  Men did not strike out against female empowerment.  Sure, some male individuals did.  But we did not march the streets by the thousands to that end.  Women did, but men did not.  So reconsider just how much you think men stand in women's way.  They really don't, and women are actually a lot more likely to check other women.  That's what I know from actually talking to women about it though, not what I just assume based on what one group of people has told me.  Believe it or not, broadening your perspective is a worthwhile pursuit.

Maria And Gianni's Channel

"We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are." Anais Nin

Consider the following stories.
I read an interview of a former professional hockey player, about his experience being the only gay athlete. He was ashamed of admiting he was gay, because of the attitude and persona in the locker rooms. So, he went through high school, on the NHL draft scout list, dating girls, and partying and drinking every night, even though he didn't really like the lifestyle. It wound up costing him his spot in the draft, as his performance slipped, and he lost the spotlight. Having missed the NHL draft, he signed on to play in European leagues, in Norway. There, he continued the charade of dating women and hiding who he was, always feeling depressed and alone. He said that the constant attitudes, and anti-homosexual remarks in the locker rooms led him to attempt suicide on several occassions. He now is sharing his story, because of how destructive those locker rooms were to him.

He had a friend who knew he was gay. His name was Brendan Burke, the son of NHL Hall of Famer, and Toronto Maple Leafs General Manager Brian Burke. Brendan too was a shoe in for the NHL Draft. The Maple Leafs loved him, and he was a welcome guest in their locker room any time. Brendan was a star in the eyes of the league he was destined to play in, and was even the subject featured on TSN discussions routinely. He was a proud ambassador of the sport, and all sports really, inspiring kids all over. They lived radically different lives. 
Shortly before Brendan's tragic death in a car accident, he told his friend on the phone, "I can't wait for the day you can come out and be as accepted by your family as I am with mine". Yes, that's right. Brendan Burke was expected to be the first openly gay player drafted into the NHL. His campaigns to show that being gay didn't mean you couldn't be an athlete, and couldn't be welcomed in the locker room were summed up in his notorious catch phrase "If you can play, you can play". Those TSN discussions, were about how this would change the NHL, having it's first openly gay hockey player. Not because people weren't ready...but because people knew there are already likely players who are. As over 70% of the NHL Players Association is from Canada, we will go ahead and use Canadian stats on it. As of 2012, 5.3% openly identified as gay in a survey. So, 5 out of every 100 are gay. The NHL had 30 teams at that time, all with rosters of 20-23 players. That means there were 600 to 700 players in the NHL at any given time (Double that if you include the entire AHL farm team roster). So, statistically speaking, there should be, roughly 30-35 players in the NHL who are gay, and another 35 or more in the AHL. Brendan Burke didn't ignite a firestorm of backlash. He didn't live a life of depression and anxiety, or victimhood because of the chauvenistic nature of professional sports. He was openly welcomed by the entire community. The news of his death shook the league. NHL teams lowered their flags, and played in honour of him for what he had accomplished for the league, despite not even being old enough to play in it. The Toronto Maple Leafs started the campagin "You can Play", taping their sticks in rainbow coloured tape and saying that their lockerroom is, and always will be a welcome place for everyone, regardless of their sexual orientation. Other teams and players followed...many. Some from the NBA, even football players, and other sports. 

Two gay men, one exact same industry and circle (many of the players in European leagues played in or with NHL players/teams too). Two radically different outcomes in life. Why?

How you are treated comes down entirely to how you expect to be. The first man tried to hide who he was. He lived a phoney life, and as such, people didn't see him as authentic. They didn't trust him. He pissed his future away drinking and partying to try and be "cool", when the rest of his teammates were abstaining (many Junior hockey teams here do not let their players drink, have a curfew, etc). He chose his path, as tragic as it was. The other, chose to be himself. He never hid who he was. He didn't worry about whether his father would reject him for being who he is, because he knew that was beyond his control, and had no reflection on him. As a result, he discovered that his father was one of the most staunch supporters he had. Did he face adversity along the way? Of course he did. We all do. But it's how we deal with it that makes all the difference. 

One girl started at the bottom of the pay in a company, as an assistant, complaining she couldn't afford to take care of her children as a single mom, and ended up quitting. Another girl started at that exact same spot, and decided that since she was a single mother, she had to fight as hard as she could to do everything she could to get her kids out of that low income life. Within a few short years, she rose to CEO of that company, starred as a venture capitalist investor on a reality TV show, and is one of the most powerful people in the business world in the country, with hundreds of millions of dollars at her disposal. 

If you feel like you are expected to act a certain way as an African American woman, then don't. Be yourself, and to hell with the stereotypes of others. It isn't a reflection of you. Of course there are people that will attempt to hold you back...there are for everyone. Oprah Winfrey faced those exact same problems as an African American woman when she started her career....in a time when neither African American, nor women, were really even considered to be able to be anchors. Yet she defied them all. 

Others can tell you all they want what you are capable of, or what you are allowed to do, or not do....but it doesn't matter, because they don't get to decide. You do.

It turned out that one of the girls in said circle thought I was stalking her, and they were making fun of me behind my back. I became a recluse, and lost trust in people outside of my family for a long time.

I’m 43 years old, autistic (not diagnosed until I was 28), and a recovering alcoholic who used to drink alone. However, I’ve not only sobered up, but I finally got out of retail a while back, and found a much better paying job. One where I’ve made some real friends among my coworkers. I’ve still never been in a relationship, but I don’t care about that anymore. If it happens, great. If not, it’s not a problem.

In my 20s, though, I was enraged over it. I wasted so much time arguing with people on the internet, to the point where it got me banned from my favorite forum at the time. I never said any of the garbage I’ve seen in this video, but I was so blinded by my anger, that i didn’t realize how I was coming off. No one wants to talk to someone who’s that big of an asshole.

I don’t condone any of the vile, sexist, or racist BS that I’ve seen on these Incel forums. Those posts make me even more angry than the kids who bullied me. Those idiots overshadow the rest of us, who are simply reaching out for understanding and compassion, in a world they feel has left them behind.

I just hope these young men find satisfaction in life a little sooner than I did.

Not because they’re “undateable” but because they don’t realize that minor changes can get them what they desire and also because they’ve put their confidence in women accepting them. Personally I focus on self improvement and  it’s been the best for me to focus on Christ instead of obsessing over if someone wants to date me or not. There is so much more to live for and the most important one is the Lord. Community is vital but without God you fall into the trap of being part of communities that turn your insecurities into your identity which is dangerous. They turn a common bond into bondage that causes you to not see your great potential. Also, sometimes rejection is protection BUT  it could also be feedback for you to see what you need to work on. Everybody has areas of improvement* and no one is exempt.

We are not born incels, their bitters experiences for reasons out of their hand make them one. Don't save them, but don't shove them away which will only cause isolation.

That would also very likely have women too afraid to speak up, because they're scared that if they do come forward and it can't be proven, that they could face punishment for actually being a victim.

text:
I have a friend that teaches 3rd grade. He was accused of assaulting and graping one of his students and the school district (my wife was serving on the school board so none of this was ever made public) was notified by the sheriff that once the DA returned from vacation that he was going to be arrested. The teacher was placed on immediate paid leave for good reasons but no arrest was ever made. Finally nearly 7 months later it was finally revealed that shortly after my friend was first placed on leave evidence was found suggesting but not providing the actual criminal was the little girls uncle. However, despite the victim recanting her original statement and a mountain of other evidence he was still considered a suspect. Therefore, because details of an active investigation are not normally shared the district was just told active investigation and the leave was continued. The stress alone during that situation nearly ruined my friends life. Thankfully no details were ever made public so he was able to return the next year. But even more important, his wife believed him and his family made it through this whole. 

We often forget how awful it is for the falsely accused. My friends story is a reminder that no arrests  have to be made and no one has to be fired for false accusations to potentially ruin someone's life. For my friend what saved his marriage is that the accusations were far beyond believable based on his character. To be clear the little girl was desperate for help but because of legitimate fear could not accuse her uncle and neither myself nor my friend blame her for what he had to endure.

I completely agree with Nate, when the facts and evidence can prove in the court of law that the accusations were made with malice then the punishment for false accusations should be the same as the punishment for the crimes they accused the actual victim of. In this case she should get the appropriate amount of jail time and be registered as a sex offender.

text:
I have a friend that teaches 3rd grade. He was accused of assaulting and graping one of his students and the school district (my wife was serving on the school board so none of this was ever made public) was notified by the sheriff that once the DA returned from vacation that he was going to be arrested. The teacher was placed on immediate paid leave for good reasons but no arrest was ever made. Finally nearly 7 months later it was finally revealed that shortly after my friend was first placed on leave evidence was found suggesting but not providing the actual criminal was the little girls uncle. However, despite the victim recanting her original statement and a mountain of other evidence he was still considered a suspect. Therefore, because details of an active investigation are not normally shared the district was just told active investigation and the leave was continued. The stress alone during that situation nearly ruined my friends life. Thankfully no details were ever made public so he was able to return the next year. But even more important, his wife believed him and his family made it through this whole. 

We often forget how awful it is for the falsely accused. My friends story is a reminder that no arrests  have to be made and no one has to be fired for false accusations to potentially ruin someone's life. For my friend what saved his marriage is that the accusations were far beyond believable based on his character. To be clear the little girl was desperate for help but because of legitimate fear could not accuse her uncle and neither myself nor my friend blame her for what he had to endure.

I completely agree with Nate, when the facts and evidence can prove in the court of law that the accusations were made with malice then the punishment for false accusations should be the same as the punishment for the crimes they accused the actual victim of. In this case she should get the appropriate amount of jail time and be registered as a sex offender.

Many of you point to an earnings gap and not a wage gap. You are right, to a certain degree, and that is that actual wage gap is around 7% in the US (as pointed in many comments here). So that means men work in fields that usually get paid more and also work more hours.

But what does this tell us? Should we regard this as normal and move on? Why would this social construct be in any way natural? 

For example, a doctoral thesis by Merja Kinnunen presents strong evidence that the original wage classifications were based on sex in the 1920s Finland (the country where I live). The reasoning went like this: men are the head of the family and the natural breadwinner, so we need to give men dominated fields higher wages (it was called "family wage"). And as females should rely on their (future) husbands for support, the female dominated fields could do with lower wages. The doctoral thesis actually cites the original wage classification reasoning that clearly uses this logic to establish the wage level for different fields.

What does this tell us? For example, both nurses and engineers study 3½ years after high school in Finland, and you can argue that even though the fields are different, they are comparably stressful and demanding. But because of the original wage classifications, which were outspokenly sexist, nurses still make a lot less than engineers in Finland.

Why is it then that women on average want to be nurses and not engineers? Because it is how they are brought up and educated & what society expects. These things are the reasons why anyone chooses any career at all. 

So to summarize. Many of you commenting on earnings gap vs wage gap are right. The wage gap is not that big. But the earnings gap is still a problem, because the wage differences between male dominated and female dominated fields are based on old sexist reasoning that is now cemented on seemingly "natural" wage differences between fields - and society at large keeps the whole construct alive and well by bringing up boys and girls so differently.

Also, on a side note, I find it to be a feminist problem that men are working so much more overtime than women. Clearly the old breadwinner-construct is still alive and well - and it's hurting men by putting unreasonable pressure on them as well as women by shoving them to lesser paid fields that are being paid less because of the breadwinner-construct to begin with. As usual with sexist societal constructs: everybody loses.

Whenever I talk about this, the discussion usually follows this path (and I swear I'm not constructing a strawman - I've had the same exact discussion at least four different times):

Them: men are being paid more because they work longer hours in jobs that are higher paid - it's not sexist
Me: did you know the male dominated jobs are higher paid because of breadwinner-construct/family wage ideal got cemented in the wage classifications nearly a hundred years ago?
Them: but men also work longer hours (ignoring previous argument)
Me: is this a good thing, though.. should we be happy with how things are now?
Them: but men are naturally inclined to work more for their families so that's why they aim for the higher paying jobs and work more overtime
Me: you started by saying wage gap isn't sexist and you ended up supporting it with a sexist argument
Them: ad hominem attack of their choice

Furthermore, we have many case studies where lower classes have had their IQ tested before and after receiving further education and we have seen the median IQ rising usually from 80 to 110 as a result. So, it begs the question, if IQ is set: how it can change in one year so drastically - and if it's not set; is it not harmful to test people and tell them it is a set feature and not to focus on education. Even more, as population education level has risen the IQ tests have gotten harder and harder; right now we'd all be geniuses if we used the Binet's original test - which was a tool to decide who needed more help with learning to get even.

So even though this feels a little bit like answering a kettle argument I will go on.

As I see it, you didn't challenge my overall argument, but did challenge three details in it: 1920s classifications are not valid today, wages are set by the capitalist system, hunter gatherer systems had labor division by sex. I feel like my original post was a very long one already, so I left out many of these things to make it more brief - but I can elaborate on them as you wish.

1920s classification are not valid today:

You are right to point out that societal changes have evened the playing field especially from the 60s onward. However, I didn't claim the situation was as dire as it was in the 1920s - I merely pointed out the fact that the system we now have is based on a very sexist system that still has some effect on our current wage gap. In the doctoral thesis I referred to earlier, we can see that each subsequent deal between employees and employers is based on the last deal. So even though we have gained a better position each time, the starting point was so bad that it hasn't been fully fixed in 9 decades.

Wages are set by the capitalist system:

Here is where we enter a culture gap. In Finland, as is true in much of Europe, wage levels are set between the worker unions, employer unions and the state. As overwhelming majority of the workforce belongs to the unions, the minimum wage levels per fields set in these negotiations are the one thing that most affects wages. The negotiations have made it visible that the previous deals have been very gendered. But perhaps we are having two separate discussions because we live in two separate cultures in regards to this issue at least.

EqualRightsAdvocate Yes, you are right. There is no law stopping them.

However, it is not as straightforward as that. I assume you are aware of the socialization process and the norm system? In short, our society teaches us a certain culture and a norm system. If we go against that norm system, we face sanctions. We we comply with that norm system, we get rewards. These are not laws, but stuff like how to dress or what to say in any given situation. 

Now, we have a lot of studies concerning how the norm system is different for males and females. Just a few short examples. In Sweden, the most equal country of all, the baby x tests found out adults treat babies fundamentally different if they think they are boys or girls. They dressed the same baby sometimes in blue and sometimes in pink and the adults acted accordingly. Dressed in blue, the baby was given rough play and shoved hammers in her hand - encouraged to be active. Dressed in pink, the baby was coddled and given dolls to caress - softly sung songs. In another study, career counselors in Finland were found out to give gendered advice to boys and girls with same type of personality and grade average: active boys were encouraged to be leaders but active girls were seen as social: so maybe fashion bloggers or hairdressers. We can see the same pattern in toy advertisements, parent expectations, popular media and teacher attitudes. 

So, yes, nothing by law stops women from entering high paid professions. That is why we have women in these professions at all. But simply being allowed to is not the same as being encouraged to. That is why we have less women in these professions. 

Also, as a male feminist I think the gendered expectations are really hurting men, as well. We see studies that show that females consider the fact how much a man earns to be more important than anything else. This societal norm puts great pressure on men to be something they maybe aren't. If you want to be a male nurse (or a stay-at-home dad), for example, you face same kind of sanctions from breaking the social norm that you would as a female being a computer scientist. So it is in everybody's interest to unmask these societal constructs and create a society where people can more freely choose based on their person, not their gender (because we have more variety inside the genders than between them).

However, I take issue on some of the larger claims you make. It is easy to assume a difference in men and women (i.e. evolution probably made us different) but harder to back it up with evidence (other than in appearance and physical capability). What you are assuming is fine as a theory but you'd need evidence for it to be credible. And here's the funny part: people are often unwilling to single out on how they think men and female are different. We very rarely see a genuine "lady brains" -argument - more often it is mystified as some big difference that cannot be tested or studied on. As such, I see little use to an assumption as that - it looks as it only serves as a political tool to sweep sexism under the rug. So it is simple: give me the evidence on how male and female brains differ on cognitive abilities and then I'll start believing that's the reason for the earnings gap. Until you do, I will hold societal constructs a more plausible reason (as briefly summarized in my response to equalrightsadvocate above).

Also, we have had a similar discussion before that now looks absurd. The difference of cultural and economic input between black and white populations begged the question: is this really because the "races" have different brains or cognitive capabilities? Scientific racism was a big thing - not only in Germany - until we got the result: skin color is as important as eye color and human DNA is astonishingly close between different populations (and the differences between populations are insignificant, relating to things like lactose intolerance and not cognitive abilities). So that was the end of scientific racism.

I do think that scientific sexism, if it ever does become a thing, will face same end result.

They also specify that the differences short-term are larger for biological families than for adoptive families.

But you also need to keep in mind that it only provides actual meaningful data from Denmark. They explain this as it being hard to get adoptive data from other countries, but what it also means is that this is just one nation we're talking about. 

So in the end, all that paper is, is a huge estimation. It even mentions that estimations from other nations differs even more, Scandinavian countries between 20-25 percent, USA being 30 percent, and Germany being 60 percent for some reason.

​ @automatic5  "Go look for something which echoes my claim" is a lousy substitute for a credible source and if you're going to present factual information (as opposed to logical deduction without any new claims even implied) the onus is on you to back it up.  This is not an insulting request but rather a key prerequisite for any intelligent discourse.

It also aids the speaker who, if not remembering and revisiting their sources, is susceptible to factual drift from forgotten context and unconscious bias.  A thing worth writing is worth writing accurately, and a thing worth reading generally relies on proof to hold that value - else the value must come from the idea independent from fact.

And beyond all that, the etiquette of intelligent discourse is itself intelligently derived from good mental economics; a writer's effort is expended once and a reader's effort is expended once for every reader.  If you don't respect your reader's attention and effort, don't expect them to respect your lack of it.

@thefalsehero  Well that is only one part of her work. 
About the U-curve, she corrected a widespread notion that the increase of labor force participation of women led to economic growth, when actually it was just technology and the industrial age. She also corrected historical underreporting of married women working (which was seldom included in census or other survey data).
More importantly, she analyzed the factors that led to women earning less in general mostly from pregnancy/childcare but also the fact that women were less inclined to get an education because they expect to become mothers and not work.
That last part is pretty important, because it shows that women becoming more educated today is a result of the previous generation’s ability to work (which she also correlates with the invention of birth control since it gives more power to women when it comes to their careers and motherhood). This shows that pay gap data is outdated, since it includes less educated women in older generations, who did not expect to work.
Goldin also analyzes historical price discrimination, which is what people think the pay gap is today, even though it’s not.
Sure you could argue that some random person could theorize this on an armchair one day, but she did the work behind the theories and informed a lot of the (educated) facts we know about wage gaps today.

text: I the 1970s when I was a young adult, almost half of us were creating alternative ways of living outside the capitalist patriarchy. My now husband and I lived a year in a 50-year-old 8x24 foot trailer and farmed tobacco and lived the whole year on $300, not counting farm expenses which we charged until our crop sold. We were burned out from a few years as a reporting/writing team working 80 hour weeks. We didn’t buy a single item that year outside food we hadn’t grown and had paid our car insurance up 18 months in advance. It was backbreaking labor for us both but was so healing. Neither of us participated in the capitalist society, the first time since we were 6 either of us hadn’t been in school or work. The point is there is a whole world we could be creating for men and women with equality and no sex roles but it is very very hard. My generation of feminists focused on getting into the world of work because without economic equality we had no power to change our own lives, much less politics and society. Both men and women now need to move to challenge capitalism. But social workers started taking peoples kids if they had well water, outside toilets and wood stoves, forcing them off communes and subsistence farms living in school busses, mud huts and old trailers. We actually got married, went to grad school and cut off our long fuzzy hair because I couldn’t get pregnant and couldn’t go to fertility treatment nor apply for adoption unless we did. We actually totally remade our selves during the decade it took us to get two babies and finalize their adoptions. Our dreams of working together and hitchhiking with babies on our backs became two frazzled parents and an infant in a 59-mile triangle, seeing each other 2-4 hours in the evening before falling into bed exhausted. We were forced apart after a decade of sharing offices at newspapers and universities to meet income requirements for a social worker. Once our second adoption was finalized he found a job that required 37 1/2 hours fulltime and I worked from home and cared for the baby and toddler. It was as close as we could get to our dream life but we shared every chore and childcare and they could go to work with dad at the tutoring/writing center any time and did sleep on his back while he taught writing classes. Those days of the 1990s are gone now and kids aren’t welcome on campus. But alternatives can be created.
